chunks.title: Orbit walls & fissures
chunks.tldr: Medial wall is paper-thin → ethmoid sinusitis spreads in. Floor breaks in blowouts. The SOF carries most of the eye-movement nerves.
points: Roof (2 bones: frontal, lesser wing of sphenoid). A hole here → pulsating proptosis without a bruit (brain pulse).
Lateral wall (2: zygomatic, greater wing). The strongest wall. The front of the globe sticks out past it.
Floor (3: maxilla, zygomatic, palatine). Weak posteromedial maxilla → blowout fracture. Maxillary cancer pushes the eye up.
Medial wall (4: maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid, sphenoid). Lamina papyracea is paper-thin → orbital cellulitis from ethmoid sinusitis.
Superior orbital fissure: top part = lacrimal, frontal, IV, superior ophthalmic vein. Bottom part (inside the ring) = III (both divisions), VI, nasociliary, sympathetics.
Inferior orbital fissure: maxillary nerve (V2), zygomatic nerve, inferior ophthalmic vein.
Optic nerve in the orbit = 25 mm, but the globe-to-canal distance is only 18 mm → spare slack for proptosis.
chunks.hook: Walls by bone count: Roof 2, Lateral 2, Floor 3, Medial 4.

cards.q: Why does ethmoid sinusitis cause orbital cellulitis so easily?
cards.a: The lamina papyracea of the medial wall is paper-thin with many foramina.

cards.q: Which nerve passes through the SOF but outside the annulus of Zinn: III, IV or VI?

chunks.title: Signs of orbital disease
chunks.tldr: Hertel >20 mm or a 2–3 mm difference = proptosis. Axial → inside the muscle cone. Dystopia → outside the cone.
points: Look from above and behind the patient to spot asymmetric proptosis.
Axial (straight forward) proptosis: intraconal mass (cavernous haemangioma, optic nerve tumour, TED).
Dystopia (pushed up, down or sideways): extraconal mass, e.g. a lacrimal gland tumour pushes the eye down and in.
Pseudoproptosis: big myopic eye, buphthalmos, lid retraction, enophthalmos on the other side.
Enophthalmos: blowout fracture, atrophy, scirrhous breast metastasis, blind babies poking their eyes (oculodigital sign).
Proptosis that gets worse with Valsalva or head-down → venous anomaly (varix).
Pulsation + bruit → carotid-cavernous fistula. Pulsation, no bruit → roof defect (e.g. NF1).
chunks.hook: Bruit = blood (CCF). No bruit = brain (roof defect).

cards.q: Hertel readings 18 and 21 mm. Significant?
cards.a: Yes: >20 mm, and a 3 mm difference.

cards.q: Enophthalmos in a woman with a history of breast cancer?

chunks.title: Restriction vs palsy & fundus clues
chunks.tldr: Forced duction tells restriction from palsy. Opticociliary shunts → think optic nerve sheath meningioma.
points: Forced duction: grab the muscle insertion with forceps and rotate. Resistance → restrictive (TED, fracture). No resistance → nerve palsy.
Differential IOP test: IOP rises ≥6 mmHg when looking toward the limited side → restriction (Braley sign).
Saccades: slow in palsy. Normal speed but a sudden stop in restriction.
Fundus: disc swelling (early compression) → optic atrophy (late), choroidal folds.
Opticociliary shunt vessels: big twisty vessels on the disc that vanish at the edge. Commonest with optic nerve sheath meningioma (also glioma, CRVO, IIH, glaucoma).
Imaging: CT for bone, trauma, abscess. MRI for the apex, intracranial spread, inflammation (STIR shows active TED).
chunks.hook: Shunts = Sheath meningioma.

cards.q: IOP rises from 16 to 24 on upgaze. What does this suggest?
cards.a: Restrictive myopathy (e.g. TED inferior rectus): positive Braley sign.

cards.q: Most common tumour with opticociliary shunts?

chunks.title: TED: who gets it & why
chunks.tldr: TED = commonest cause of proptosis in adults (one or both eyes). Smoking is the biggest risk factor. Radioiodine can make it worse.
points: Graves disease: IgG antibodies switch on TSH receptors → hyperthyroid. Women, aged 40s–50s.
Body clues: weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, goitre, acropachy (clubbing-like), pretibial myxoedema.
TED can also happen when euthyroid or hypothyroid, and can come before any thyroid problem.
Smoking = biggest risk. More cigarettes = more risk. Stopping helps.
Women 5× more (because Graves is more common in women).
Radioiodine can worsen TED → give oral steroid cover if they already have eye disease.
Mechanism: antibodies hit orbital fibroblasts → glycosaminoglycans soak up water → muscles swell (up to 8×) → later fibrosis → restriction.
chunks.hook: TED's 3 'S': Smoking, Steroid cover for radioiodine, Swollen muscles.

cards.q: Biggest modifiable risk factor for TED?
TED patient needs radioiodine. What else do you give?
cards.a: A short course of oral steroids.

chunks.title: TED signs: lids, proptosis, muscles
chunks.tldr: Two phases: red, hot, active (1–3 years) → white, burnt-out fibrosis. Commonest motility problem = can't look up (tight inferior rectus).
points: Soft tissue: red over the recti insertions, puffy lids, chemosis, fat prolapse, dry eye, SLK.
Lid retraction (~50% of Graves). Dalrymple = retraction looking straight ahead. Kocher = frightened stare. von Graefe = lid lag on downgaze.
Proptosis: axial, often permanent → exposure keratopathy, ulcers.
Restrictive myopathy (30–50%). Muscles most often involved: Inferior rectus → Medial → Superior → Lateral ('I'M SLow').
Tight IR → can't look up (mimics SR palsy). Tight MR → can't abduct (mimics a VI palsy).
On scans: muscle belly swollen, tendon spared.
EUGOGO severity: sight-threatening (optic neuropathy or corneal breakdown) / moderate–severe / mild.
chunks.hook: I'M SLow: Inferior, Medial, Superior, Lateral rectus.

cards.q: Lid lag on downgaze in TED is called?
Most commonly involved muscle in TED, and the resulting motility defect?
TED vs myositis on imaging?
cards.a: TED spares the tendon; myositis usually involves it.

chunks.title: TED optic neuropathy: don't miss it
chunks.tldr: Fat muscles squeeze the nerve at the apex, even without much proptosis. Colour desaturation is the most sensitive sign.
points: Up to 6% of TED patients.
Squeezed at the orbital apex by swollen recti. Tight orbits (little proptosis) are actually more at risk.
Signs: ↓VA (not always), colour desaturation, ↓brightness, RAPD, central/paracentral field loss.
The disc may be normal, swollen, or (rarely) pale.
Can look like POAG (field defects + high IOP from tight muscles).
Teach patients to check themselves: cover one eye, read small print, compare colour on the TV.
chunks.hook: TED + colours look washed out = emergency for the nerve.

cards.q: Most sensitive early sign of TED optic neuropathy?
Can compressive optic neuropathy occur in TED without proptosis?

chunks.title: Treating TED
chunks.tldr: Stop smoking. Mild → lubricants. Active moderate–severe (CAS ≥3/7) → IV methylprednisolone. Surgery order: orbit → squint → lids.
points: Everyone: stop smoking, control the thyroid.
Mild: lubricants, sleep with the head raised, tape the lids, selenium.
Clinical Activity Score (1 point each): pain at rest, pain on eye movement, lid swelling, lid redness, conjunctival redness, chemosis, swollen caruncle/plica. ≥3/7 = active.
Active moderate–severe: IV methylprednisolone 0.5 g weekly × 6, then 0.25 g weekly × 6. Max total <8 g (liver). Oral steroids are the alternative.
Orbital radiotherapy: add-on, works in ~6 weeks. Avoid in diabetics (retinopathy) and young patients.
Teprotumumab (IGF-1R blocker) reduces proptosis and CAS. Rituximab is another option.
Optic neuropathy: pulsed IV steroids. If no response → urgent orbital decompression.
Burnt-out phase, in order: decompression → squint surgery (stable 6–12 months; recess only, never resect; adjustable sutures) → lid surgery last.
chunks.hook: Surgery order O-S-L: Orbit, Squint, Lids. Like getting dressed: trousers before shoes.
pearls: Decompression: 1 wall (deep lateral) ≈ 4–5 mm, least diplopia. 3 walls ≈ 6–10 mm, more diplopia and infraorbital numbness.

cards.q: Name 3 CAS items.
cards.a: Any of: spontaneous pain, pain on eye movement, lid swelling, lid redness, conjunctival redness, chemosis, caruncle/plica swelling.

cards.q: TED strabismus surgery: recess or resect?
cards.a: Recess only (usually IR/MR), with adjustable sutures.

cards.q: Why is orbital radiotherapy avoided in diabetics?

chunks.title: Preseptal vs orbital cellulitis
chunks.tldr: Preseptal: swollen lid but normal vision, pupils, eye movements, no proptosis. Any of those abnormal → orbital cellulitis → admit + CT.
points: Preseptal: in front of the septum. Staph/Strep. From a cut, insect bite, stye, dacryocystitis, URTI.
Preseptal: oral co-amoxiclav. Check tetanus. Imaging only if unsure.
Orbital: behind the septum. Mostly kids, usually from ethmoid sinusitis. Strep pneumoniae, Staph aureus, Strep pyogenes, H. influenzae.
Orbital signs: fever, pain on eye movement, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, chemosis, ↓VA, colour loss, RAPD.
Complications: optic neuropathy, subperiosteal abscess (usually medial), meningitis, brain abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Treat: admit, CT of orbit + sinuses + brain, IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftazidime + metronidazole) until fever-free for 4 days, ENT review, check the nerve every 4 h. Drain an abscess.
chunks.hook: The septum is the wall. Behind the wall = the eye is in trouble.

cards.q: Swollen red lid, VA 6/6, full motility, no proptosis. Diagnosis?
Commonest source of orbital cellulitis?

chunks.title: Mucormycosis
chunks.tldr: Diabetic ketoacidosis or immunosuppressed + black eschar on the palate, nose or lids = mucor. Often fatal.
points: Fungus (Mucoraceae) breathed in → sinuses → orbit → brain.
Invades blood vessels → clots → tissue dies (black eschar).
Slower than bacterial cellulitis. Can cause retinal artery occlusion and multiple cranial nerve palsies.
Treat: fix the DKA, IV antifungal (amphotericin), debride dead tissue. May need exenteration. Hyperbaric O₂ can help.
chunks.hook: Diabetic + black spot = mucor.

cards.q: Black necrotic palate in a patient with DKA and orbital signs?

chunks.title: Orbital inflammation (pseudotumour) & myositis
chunks.tldr: IOID = painful, inflamed orbit with no infection or cancer. Diagnosis of exclusion → biopsy before steroids if it's atypical.
points: Painful red swelling, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia ± optic nerve problems. Adults: one side. Kids: can be both sides + fever.
CT: ill-defined fuzzy orbital tissue.
Course: goes away, keeps coming back, or scars into a 'frozen orbit'.
Treat: watch, then NSAIDs, then oral pred 1–1.5 mg/kg (only once infection, lymphoma, GPA are excluded). Radiotherapy if no response in 2 weeks. Methotrexate, etc.
Orbital myositis: young adult, painful diplopia, redness over one muscle. Scan: muscle and tendon swollen (TED spares the tendon).
Myositis responds dramatically to steroids, but 50% recur.
chunks.hook: Myositis takes the tendon too. Thyroid leaves the tendon alone.

cards.q: Why confirm the diagnosis before steroids in suspected IOID?
cards.a: Steroids can mask infection, lymphoma or GPA.

cards.q: Imaging difference between orbital myositis and TED?
cards.a: Myositis involves the tendon; TED spares it.

chunks.title: Dacryoadenitis, Tolosa–Hunt, GPA
chunks.tldr: Swollen lacrimal gland → S-shaped lid. Painful ophthalmoplegia at the apex → Tolosa–Hunt. Both orbits + sinuses → GPA (cANCA).
points: Acute dacryoadenitis: idiopathic or viral (mumps, EBV, CMV). Tender gland, S-shaped ptosis, eye pushed down and in.
Chronic, two-sided gland swelling: sarcoid, Sjögren, TED.
Bone erosion on CT → tumour, not inflammation.
Tolosa–Hunt: granulomatous inflammation of the cavernous sinus/SOF/apex. One-sided pain + III/IV/VI palsies + V1/V2 numbness. Rule everything else out. Responds to steroids, relapses.
GPA (Wegener): orbit (often both sides) spread from the sinuses/nose. Also scleritis, PUK. Test cANCA. Treat with cyclophosphamide + steroids.
chunks.hook: Bilateral orbital inflammation + bad sinuses = GPA until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Serology for granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
Painful ophthalmoplegia + V1 numbness responding dramatically to steroids?

chunks.title: Cavernous sinus thrombosis & CCF
chunks.tldr: Direct CCF = trauma, pulsatile proptosis + bruit + chemosis. Indirect (dural) = slow red eye with corkscrew vessels, often missed.
points: Cavernous sinus thrombosis: from face/sinus/orbit infection. Both eyes proptosed, chemosis, III–VI palsies, very sick. 20% die even with treatment. IV antibiotics.
Direct CCF: high flow, ICA tears into the sinus. 75% trauma, or a ruptured aneurysm (middle-aged hypertensive woman).
Direct signs: pulsatile proptosis, bruit (stops when you press the carotid), haemorrhagic chemosis, big epibulbar vessels, ↑IOP, anterior segment ischaemia, CRVO.
VI nerve is hit most (it floats free in the sinus). III and IV sit in the wall, so they're safer.
Indirect (dural) CCF: low flow through meningeal branches. Slowly red eye(s), corkscrew vessels, ↑IOP (higher on that side), big ocular pulse on applanation.
Scan: enlarged superior ophthalmic vein, fat muscles. Gold standard = angiography.
Treat: direct → endovascular coil/balloon. Indirect → up to 50% close by themselves. Cortical venous drainage = stroke risk, refer urgently.
chunks.hook: Red eye that never gets better + corkscrew vessels + high IOP → dural CCF.

cards.q: Triad of a direct CCF?
Which cranial nerve is most often palsied in CCF, and why?
cards.a: VI: it floats free inside the cavernous sinus.

cards.q: Key CT/MRI sign of CCF?

chunks.title: Dermoid, dacryops, mucocoele, encephalocoele
chunks.tldr: Kid with a smooth lump at the upper-outer orbit = dermoid. Take it out in one piece: if it bursts, it causes nasty inflammation.
points: Dermoid cyst: choristoma (normal tissue in the wrong place). Lined with skin, contains hair and glands. Among the commonest orbital tumours in kids.
Superficial dermoid: babies, firm 1–2 cm lump, usually superotemporal, fixed to bone, back edge easy to feel.
Deep dermoid: teens/adults, slow proptosis, or sudden inflammation if it ruptures. Can go through bone.
Remove intact. Leaking keratin → granulomatous inflammation.
Dacryops: cyst of the lacrimal gland ducts, bulges into the upper fornix.
Sinus mucocoele: blocked sinus (usually frontal/ethmoid) slowly erodes into the orbit → dystopia, diplopia, watering. CT shows thinned bone.
Encephalocoele: brain/meninges poking through a skull defect. Front ones push the eye down and out. Back ones (NF1) push it down. Swells when crying, pulsates with no bruit.
chunks.hook: Dermoid = a little skin bag in the wrong place. Don't pop it.

cards.q: Commonest location of a superficial orbital dermoid?
Why must a dermoid be removed intact?
cards.a: Rupture releases keratin → severe granulomatous inflammation.

chunks.title: Varices & lymphangioma
chunks.tldr: Varix = proptosis that comes and goes with Valsalva/head-down. Lymphangioma = child with sudden painful proptosis from a bleed ('chocolate cyst').
points: Orbital varices: floppy, low-flow veins. Usually upper nasal.
Proptosis on and off, no pulse or bruit, worse with coughing, straining, head-down.
Scans: phleboliths (little calcified clots). Long-standing → fat atrophy → enophthalmos + deep sulcus.
Complications: bleed, clot, optic nerve squeeze. Surgery is hard (they bleed easily).
Lymphangioma: kids. Bluish soft masses in front, or deep with a sudden bleed → chocolate cyst.
Not encapsulated, infiltrates tissue → hard to remove. Drain bad cysts or use CO₂ laser.
chunks.hook: Varix: Valsalva. Lymphangioma: Little kid, sudden bLeed.

cards.q: Proptosis that appears when the patient bends forward, no bruit?
Child with sudden painful proptosis after a cold, MRI shows a blood-filled cyst?

chunks.title: Capillary haemangioma (baby)
chunks.tldr: Commonest orbital tumour in children. Grows fast, then shrinks (75% gone by age 7). Treat for amblyopia: propranolol/timolol.
points: Girls 3:1. Noticed in the first months (30% at birth).
Surface = bright red strawberry. Deeper = blue/purple. Swells when crying. No pulse or bruit.
Many lesions / big ones → check for visceral lesions: Kasabach–Merritt (low platelets, up to 50% mortality), heart failure, PHACE syndrome.
Grows for 3–6 months, then slowly fades: 30% gone by age 3, 75% by age 7.
Treat if: amblyopia (from astigmatism, covering the pupil, or squint), nerve compression, exposure.
Oral propranolol (paediatrician) or topical timolol = first choice.
Steroid injection works, but don't inject deep (risk of CRAO). Also laser, interferon.
chunks.hook: Baby + strawberry = beta-blocker. The worry is amblyopia, not cancer.

cards.q: Main indication to treat a periocular capillary haemangioma?
First-line treatment?
cards.a: Beta-blocker: oral propranolol or topical timolol.

chunks.title: Cavernous haemangioma (adult)
chunks.tldr: Commonest benign orbital tumour in adults: middle-aged woman, slow axial proptosis, well-defined oval intraconal mass. Easy to remove.
points: ~70% women. Can grow faster in pregnancy.
Sits inside the muscle cone, behind the globe → axial proptosis, choroidal folds, disc oedema.
At the apex it can squeeze the nerve with little proptosis. Gaze-evoked blur.
CT/MRI: well-circumscribed oval, fills slowly with contrast.
Often found by chance → watch. Symptomatic → excise (encapsulated, comes out easily).
chunks.hook: Capillary = Child. Cavernous = Can be a mum (middle-aged woman).

cards.q: Most common benign orbital tumour in adults?
Gaze-evoked transient blur + slowly progressive axial proptosis in a 45-year-old woman?

chunks.title: Pleomorphic adenoma vs carcinoma
chunks.tldr: Benign: painless, >1 year, smooth bone dent → excise whole, don't biopsy. Malignant: painful, quick, bone eroded → biopsy.
points: Pleomorphic adenoma: commonest lacrimal gland epithelial tumour. Young to middle-aged adults.
Slow, painless, >12 months. Pushes the eye down and in (inferonasal dystopia).
CT: smooth round mass, bone indented, not destroyed.
Don't biopsy → it seeds and recurs, and can turn malignant. Remove intact via lateral orbitotomy.
Lacrimal carcinoma: adenoid cystic (50%) is the commonest. High mortality.
Clues: short history, pain, numbness (lacrimal nerve), old adenoma that suddenly grows, or recurrences after piecemeal removal.
CT: irregular edge, bone erosion, calcification.
Adenoid cystic spreads along nerves → into the cavernous sinus. Often needs exenteration. Poor prognosis.
chunks.hook: Painless + slow = leave it whole. Pain + bone erosion = cancer.

cards.q: Why avoid incisional biopsy of a suspected pleomorphic adenoma?
cards.a: Seeding → recurrence and possible malignant change.

cards.q: Commonest lacrimal gland carcinoma, and its special way of spreading?

chunks.title: Optic nerve glioma vs sheath meningioma
chunks.tldr: Glioma = child (~6 y), NF1, fusiform nerve. Meningioma = middle-aged woman, NF2, tram-track calcification, shunt vessels. Both: vision drops before proptosis.
points: Glioma: pilocytic astrocytoma, median age 6.5. 30% have NF1 (they do better).
Vision loss → proptosis (often pushed down/out). Disc swollen → pale. Can spread to the chiasm/hypothalamus.
MRI/CT: fusiform (spindle-shaped) nerve enlargement.
Treat: watch with serial MRI. Surgery (loses the vision in that eye) if growing toward the chiasm. Chemo/radio.
Sheath meningioma: middle-aged women. More aggressive in kids. Linked with NF2.
Hoyt–Spencer triad: slow vision loss, optic atrophy, opticociliary shunts.
CT: thickened, calcified sheath ('tram-track'). MRI is best.
Treat: watch, or fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy (saves vision). Surgery if blind or spreading into the skull.
Plexiform neurofibroma (NF1): 'bag of worms', S-shaped lid. Isolated neurofibroma: adults, easy to remove.
chunks.hook: Glioma = Girl/boy (child), NF1. Meningioma = Mum (middle-aged woman), NF2.

cards.q: Hoyt–Spencer triad?
cards.a: Progressive visual loss, optic atrophy, opticociliary shunts (optic nerve sheath meningioma).

cards.q: Optic nerve glioma is associated with which neurofibromatosis?

chunks.title: Orbital lymphoma
chunks.tldr: Older adult, painless, rubbery 'salmon' mass that moulds around things. Usually B-cell non-Hodgkin. Biopsy + whole-body staging.
points: ~8% of extranodal lymphomas are around the eye. 80% B-cell NHL.
Slow, often painless. Rubbery mass, can be in the orbit, lacrimal gland, or conjunctiva.
Many 'primary' cases later show up elsewhere in the body → systemic workup (haematology).
MRI moulds around structures. Biopsy for diagnosis.
Treat: radiotherapy (localised), chemo (widespread), rituximab.
Conjunctiva-only and small lesions do best.
chunks.hook: Old + painless + rubbery = lymphoma.

cards.q: Most orbital lymphomas are which type?

chunks.title: Rhabdomyosarcoma
chunks.tldr: Commonest primary orbital cancer in children (~7 years). Fast proptosis that looks like cellulitis but the skin isn't warm.
points: From cells that can become striated muscle. 90% under 16.
Embryonal (85%): good prognosis. Alveolar: worse (specific chromosome translocations).
Usually superonasal/superior. Rapid proptosis, red swollen skin, not warm. Diplopia more than pain.
CT/MRI: ill-defined mass, can destroy bone.
Urgent biopsy. Check lung and bone for spread.
Treat: chemo + radiotherapy (± debulking). Orbit-confined disease does well.
chunks.hook: Kid with 'orbital cellulitis' that isn't hot and doesn't respond → think rhabdo.

cards.q: Most common primary orbital malignancy in children?
Which subtype has the best prognosis?

chunks.title: Metastases & invasion from nearby
chunks.tldr: Adult orbital mets: breast (up to 70%), lung, prostate. Scirrhous breast → enophthalmos. Child: neuroblastoma → black eyes + proptosis.
points: Adult primaries: breast, bronchus, prostate, melanoma, GI, kidney. Mostly palliative radiotherapy (median survival ~4 months).
Signs: proptosis, dystopia, firm orbit that resists push-back, cranial nerve palsies, or enophthalmos (scirrhous).
Neuroblastoma: abdominal (adrenal) primary in young kids. Sudden proptosis + lid bruising ('raccoon eyes'), can be both sides.
Myeloid sarcoma (chloroma): green tumour, leukaemia, age ~7.
Langerhans cell histiocytosis: lytic bone lesion, superotemporal, kids.
Maxillary carcinoma: pushes the eye up, epistaxis, facial pain. Ethmoid → lateral dystopia.
Sphenoid-wing meningioma, fibrous dysplasia (McCune–Albright if polyostotic), lid/conjunctival/intraocular cancers can also invade.
chunks.hook: Child + black eyes + proptosis with no trauma → neuroblastoma.

cards.q: Commonest primary site for adult orbital metastases?
Upward dystopia + epistaxis + facial pain?

chunks.title: Enucleation, evisceration, exenteration
chunks.tldr: Enucleation = remove the globe (tumour). Evisceration = remove the contents, keep the sclera (blind painful eye, never with tumour). Exenteration = remove everything in the orbit.
points: Enucleation: intraocular cancer (sent whole to the lab), severe trauma (to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia).
Evisceration: blind painful eye. Better movement (muscles left in place). Not if malignancy is suspected.
Exenteration: orbital cancer or invasion, mucormycosis. Prosthesis on glasses, glue, or magnets.
Orbital implant replaces volume. Porous (hydroxyapatite, polyethylene) lets tissue grow in → better movement.
PESS (post-enucleation socket syndrome): not enough volume → deep sulcus, ptosis, enophthalmos.
Extrusion: avoid by placing the implant deep with good tissue cover.
Conformer first → prosthesis mould at 6–8 weeks.
Cosmetic shell: sits over a phthisical eye.
chunks.hook: E-nucleation = Eye out. E-visceration = Empty the eye. Ex-enteration = Everything out.

cards.q: Why is evisceration contraindicated with suspected intraocular tumour?
cards.a: It disrupts the specimen for histology and may spread tumour.

cards.q: Deep upper sulcus, ptosis, enophthalmos after enucleation?

chunks.title: Craniosynostoses: Crouzon, Apert, Pfeiffer
chunks.tldr: Skull sutures close too early → shallow orbits → proptosis + hypertelorism. Crouzon and Apert = FGFR2. Apert = fused fingers.
points: Crouzon: AD, FGFR2. Midface underdevelopment, prominent jaw, proptosis, hypertelorism, V-pattern exotropia.
Vision risks: exposure keratopathy, optic atrophy (papilloedema, sleep apnoea).
Apert: the most severe. Conical skull, parrot-beak nose, syndactyly, developmental delay. Mostly sporadic (older parents). FGFR2.
Pfeiffer: down-slanting fissures, broad big toes and thumbs. AD.
chunks.hook: Apert = Attached fingers. Pfeiffer = big Feet (toes).

cards.q: Craniosynostosis with syndactyly?
Gene in Crouzon and Apert?
